seoDescription: Learn how to build dynamic web pages with the Django Template Language (DTL). This tutorial moves beyond simple `HttpResponse` to demonstrate how to render full HTML files. Discover how to create and configure a `templates` directory, use the `render()` function in your views, and pass dynamic data from your Python code to your HTML templates. Master the core concepts of separating logic from presentation by using DTL's variable syntax (`{{ variable }}`) to create flexible, data-driven web applications in Django.

summary:
## The Problem with `HttpResponse` Directly embedding HTML inside a Python view using `HttpResponse` is not a scalable or maintainable solution for building web pages. - It mixes presentation logic (HTML) with business logic (Python). - It becomes very difficult to manage complex HTML structures within Python strings. ## Introduction to Django Templates Django provides a powerful templating system to separate the design of a web page from its data. - **Templates** are text files (like HTML) that contain both static layout and special syntax for inserting dynamic content. - **Django Template Language (DTL)** is the syntax Django uses to process templates. It includes tags for variables, loops, conditional logic, and more. ## Implementing Templates: A Step-by-Step Guide 1. **Create a `templates` Directory**: In your project's root directory, create a new folder named `templates`. This folder will store all your HTML template files. 2. **Create an HTML File**: Inside the `templates` directory, create your HTML file (e.g., `home.html`). You can write standard HTML here. 3. **Configure `settings.py`**: You must tell Django where to find your templates. In `settings.py`, modify the `TEMPLATES` setting: ```python TEMPLATES = [ { ... 'DIRS': [os.path.join(BASE_DIR, 'templates')], ... }, ] ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > The `DIRS` key tells Django to look for templates in the specified directory at the project level. 4. **Update `views.py`**: Change your view function to render the template instead of returning a simple `HttpResponse`. - Instead of `HttpResponse`, use the `render()` function. - The `render()` function takes the `request` object and the name of the template file as arguments. ```python from django.shortcuts import render def home(request): return render(request, 'home.html') ``` ## Passing Dynamic Data to Templates To make pages dynamic, you pass data from your view to the template. - Data is passed as a dictionary, often called the **context**. - This dictionary is the third argument to the `render()` function. - **In `views.py`**: ```python def home(request): # Data can come from a database, an API, etc. return render(request, 'home.html', {'name': 'Kiran'}) ``` - **In `home.html`**: Use double curly braces `{{ }}` to access and display variables from the context. ```html

Hello {{ name }}!

``` > [!TIP] > The `{{ variable_name }}` syntax tells DTL to replace the placeholder with the value of the corresponding key from the context dictionary. ## Template Engines - Django's built-in template engine (**DTL**) is the default. - Other template engines like **Jinja2** can also be configured and used with Django.

## Recap: Request Flow and HttpResponse

Welcome back everyone. My name is Navin Reddy and let's continue with this series on Django. Till this point, we were able to print "Hello World" on the screen. And that too, the page we have printed is not a static page, right? So what we have done is the moment you send a request to a page... so what page I'm talking about? So this is what I was talking about. The moment you go to your browser when you say localhost or the IP address, colon, 8000, you will get "Hello World" because this is your home page, right?

So in your Django, what we are doing is the moment you send a request, it will go to the URLs of your project where you have mentioned that whenever someone calls for the admin, this is what it will handle. But we are not doing that. We want to handle for the home page, and that will be handled by `calc.urls`, which is here. So we have one more `urls.py` in our app. Now, the question is, why don't we do everything in this URL? Because we can have multiple apps, right? And every app will have its own URL, and it makes sense to do that because it will be isolated. So if you touch one thing, it will not affect the other one. It will be easier to manage.

So in the `urls.py`, you can see we are saying again `path` and then we are saying for the home page, we have a function named as `home`. So if you go to `views.py`, which is your Python file for views, here we are saying this is a function `home`. The moment it gets called, you just have to send a response, which is `HttpResponse`, and you have to send "Hello World", and that's what we are able to see.

## From Static Text to Dynamic Templates

But hold on. If you talk about the real projects, if we talk about the actual websites, you don't actually print only one text. You might want to print multiple texts, you want to print an image, or you want to do some amazing UI style. Don't worry, I'm not going to do that here. We are not going to create a good-looking website. We just want to pick up a simple web page. Even when you say web page, it will have certain HTML tags, right? For the title, for the background color, I mean if you want to change the background color, I know how to do that, right? Okay. So you can change the background color and then you can also have some amazing font, right? If you want to use a big heading, small heading, so of course that should be done in HTML. Now how will you use HTML here?

So let's say I want to increase the font size of it, or maybe I want to set it h1. So yes, you can do that. You can actually type h1 here. So before "Hello World" you can say `<h1>` and after world you can say `<h1>` close. This is perfectly possible, but is it logical? Because if you go to a browser, it will solve your work. You can see, refresh, you got "Hello World" in a big font. But what if you want to create a big page? I mean, multiple tags? So it doesn't make sense to type all the tags here. So what we should do, we should be creating a separate page, a home page which will have a lot of HTML tags. But don't you think the moment you create a new HTML page it will be a static page? Once you specify the content, we cannot change it. It's static, right? We want to make it dynamic.

And that's where in Django we have this amazing concept called templates. So you can imagine in a template what we can do is we can have a HTML page, and in that we can have a dynamic content. The layout will be fixed. You can change the layout or you can make it static, that's your choice. So imagine the background color will be fixed, everything, the entire layout will be fixed, but the data will change. And yes, that is possible. So in Django, we have a concept of DTL, which is Django Template Language.

## Creating Your First HTML Template

We all have one more option there. We can also use Jinja, but again, we'll talk about that later. As of now, let's focus on templates. In fact, if you go to settings, we have seen this right? We have templates here, and here we are using Django templates, right? So using this, you can actually achieve that.

Now, to see that, we have to actually create a page, right? So where you will create a page? Normally, you can create a page outside the app or in general, the root directory. So that's the root directory here. So I will just come back here. So I just want to create a folder where I will put all the pages. Now, what name I should be giving it? So you can give any name to it. You can say 'pages', you can say 'templates', so that's your choice. You can have anything. So I would say 'templates' here, since we are using DTL. In this templates folder, I want to create a file, which is `home.html`. So let's do that. So we click on 'Add File' here, and we'll say `home.html`. And this is where you will print "Hello World", but this time, of course, I will be using h1 tag. And I will type "Hello World", but just to get a different text because you might even not be knowing that something has changed. So what I will do is I will say some exclamation mark because in the actual output here, we don't have exclamation marks. So now we know when things are changing, right? So you can see we got "Hello World" and then at the end we are getting some exclamation marks. So how will you call this `home.html`? So for that, we had to do some changes.

## Configuring Templates and Rendering a Page

Because if you go to your browser and if you say refresh, nothing is happening, right? So the first thing you have to change is your settings file. So if you go back here and if you say settings, this is where you have to do some changes, okay?

Now what change? So you have to change your this `DIRS` file which is... which is actually directory file. So you have to specify the path of the template, because where you will search it? Because the moment you load this application, your Django should know where you have all the templates. So let's specify the path here. To do that, you have to say `os.path.join`, and in this you have to specify in the bracket, you have to specify two things. First the base directory, so you can simply say `BASE_DIR`, and here you have to mention the folder name where you have all the files. So you can say we have those things in 'templates', and your job is done. So you have specified the path now.

So you have to also change your `views.py` file because here we are saying `HttpResponse` and we are printing the text. We don't want to do that. We want to call the HTML page, and to achieve that, instead of saying `HttpResponse`, we have to say `render`, because you have to render your template. Because template is just a file and it might have some dynamic content, so you have to merge it, right? you have to compose your static content and the dynamic content. And that is what is rendering, but we are not doing that as of now, right? We have, we don't have dynamic content. We'll do that, but of course we have to use `render` because that's something works.

## Passing Dynamic Data to Templates

So in this `render`, we have to first pass the object of request. Because again, we will use this request object later. As of now, let's pass a request object, and then you have to also mention the page you want to call. So of course we want to call `home.html`, and that's it, your job is done.

So if I go back to my browser, I hope this will work. Let's refresh. Can you see that? We got a dynamic contact. We are calling that `home.html` and you can also see that we got exclamation marks there. But hold on, we are talking about dynamic content. Why? What if you want to use dynamic content here? So let's say instead of saying "Hello World", I want to print "Hello Naveen" here. Is it possible? Yes, we can do that.

But I want this name to be dynamic. So what we can do is instead of having this name on this page, let's go to view. Now this is your Python code, right? So you can have any... you can do any operation here. So maybe you can also fetch this name from a database. So if you want to do that, you can simply pass the name here as well. So you can... you can use a curly bracket here and specify the name, give a colon, and the name we are passing is let's say Naveen. So I want to use this name in my HTML. So we are passing some JSON format here, all the data. You can simply say go back to your `home.html` and here we want to use that stuff. So to achieve that, we can simply use two curly brackets and here we can specify a name. Now that makes it dynamic. I will talk about what did those curly brackets mean, but let me just check if it is working. And it's working again, so you can see we got Naveen.

The amazing thing is if you go back to your views and if you change the name... again, this name can be from anywhere. It can be from the internet, it can be from live streaming. So let's say if you are sending a huge amount of data, you can pick up any name and you can print it here. As of now let's keep it, let's keep it any name. So let's go with Kiran. And now if I go back, let's refresh. So you can see we got Kiran. We are not changing anything in the `home.html`, we are doing that in the Python code. Right? That's what we mean when you say dynamic content.

## Understanding DTL Syntax and Conclusion

Now this curly bracket here, it simply means that the code which we are writing here is dynamic. Okay. So this is the Jinja pattern what you say, or Jinja template. Now if you're coming from JSP or PHP, we have the same concept there as well. Now this is only for the variable. Can we use actual code? Can we do operations here? And the answer is yes, you can also do operations here. But how to do that, that we'll see later.

So I hope you are enjoying this. We have just created some dynamic content using templates. So this is your DTL, which is Django Template Language. Also, we can also use Jinja. And in fact, we have multiple engines. One is the Django template, which is by default. You can also use Jinja, but we will see that later. As of now, this is working. So I hope you enjoyed this video. Let me know in the comment section and do subscribe for further videos. Bye bye.
